To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the ingestion of sodium acetate prior to exercise reduces the rate of fat oxidation at the onset of exercise and increases carbohydrate oxidation during the initial 15 min of moderate-intensity cycling.

ingestion of a dose of 2 g·kg-1 of sodium acetate 90 min before exercise at 50 % VO2max decreased fat oxidation and increased carbohydrate oxidation during the first 30 min of exercise compared with a similar dose of sodium bicarbonate.
acetate ingestion suppresses fat oxidation at rest and in the first 15 mins of moderate-intensity cycling, but not during the final 75 mins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of sodium acetates ingestion on the metabolic and hormonal response to prolonged moderate intensity exercise.
the effect of short chain fatty acid (SCFA) ingestion upon substrate metabolism in humans.
understanding how exercise training and nutrition interact to influence metabolic and physiological adaptations in the body.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
acetate supplementation does not improve exercise performance.
acetate ingestion at rest or during exercise does not affect carbohydrate utilization, and that the effect of acetate on substrate utilization during exercise is dependent upon exercise intensity.
acetate is not a useful ergogenic aid for athletes performing moderate-intensity endurance exercise.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
sodium acetate ingestion increases carbohydrate oxidation at the onset of exercise, but does not affect fat oxidation.
sodium acetate ingestion suppresses fat oxidation at rest and during the initial stages of prolonged moderate-intensity cycling exercise.
acetate ingestion increases carbohydrate oxidation and suppresses fat oxidation during moderate-intensity exercise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ingestion of sodium salts of short chain fatty acids can be used to manipulate substrate metabolism in a way that may benefit performance in endurance sports.
sodium acetate ingestion does not appear to be beneficial for endurance performance, at least at rest and in the initial stages of exercise.
the ingestion of acetate before exercise can increase carbohydrate oxidation and reduce fat oxidation at the onset of exercise and throughout exercise.
